answer:
Here is the complete breakdown of hooks and the "lock-in zone" according to the source material.

---

### 1. Interrupt Theory & Hook Psychology
Social media feeds operate like a fast-moving highway where viewers scroll mindlessly [1]. To capture attention, a hook must hit a **freeze point**—yanking the emergency brake on the viewer's thumb and triggering an **orienting response** (an involuntary neurological reaction to a new stimulus, like spotting a wolf in your backyard) [1]. 

To freeze the scroll, every hook must prompt and answer two questions in the viewer's mind within milliseconds [2]:
1. **What is the video about?** (**Subject**)
2. **What will I get if I keep watching?** (**Outcome**)

---

### 2. The Four S's of Hook Writing
To consistently trigger an orienting response, a hook requires four core ingredients [2]:
* **Subject**: A crystal-clear anchor (person, object, place, or mission) so the viewer instantly knows what is being discussed [2].
* **Stakes**: The outcome that gives viewers a reason to care [2]. In entertainment, this is curiosity (e.g., *"Will MrBeast outshoot Ronaldo?"*) [3]. In educational content, it is a desired outcome (e.g., more views, skills, money, or time back) [3].
* **Speed**: Delivering the subject and stakes in as few words as possible [3]. This is about word **compression**, not talking unnaturally fast [3]. The brain's working memory acts like Pac-Man eating dots—it can only hold a few words at once while mapping sentence context [3, 4].
* **Simplicity**: Simple words with a single, unambiguous interpretation [4]. Avoid clever wordplay or vague setups [4]. If a viewer has to pause and think for even half a second, temporary confusion will cause them to scroll away [4].

---

### 3. The Triple Hook Framework & Visual Alignment
A complete hook is composed of three synchronized layers (plus an optional caption hook) [5, 6]:
1. **Text Hook**: On-screen title text (distinct from standard captions) [5, 7].
2. **Spoken Hook**: The verbal line spoken out loud [5, 6].
3. **Visual Hook**: The visual imagery shown during the opening seconds [5, 6].

**The Alignment Rule**: All three hooks **must align perfectly** [8]. If a viewer watches the visual without sound, they should be able to guess the spoken and text hooks, and vice versa [8]. Misalignment creates cognitive confusion and is the single most common reason business content fails [8]. 

Visual hooks are particularly critical because people's eyes perceive images faster than their ears process audio [9]. Creators should **show while they tell** [10] (for instance, showing a vivid red strawberry on screen before explaining strawberry growing techniques) [9, 10].

---

### 4. Text Hook Copywriting Rules & Design
Text hooks are the most influential component because the viewer's eyes hunt for text and process power phrases faster than they can comprehend images [7].

#### Substance Formula
A text hook should pair a **Subject Repeater** (the specific name, technical term, or proper noun) with one of three teasers [11, 12]:
* **Subject Repeater + Pain Point Reminder**: e.g., *"People Pleasing"* (Cat's viral video) [12, 13].
* **Subject Repeater + Desired Outcome Teaser**: e.g., *"ChatGPT will sell things for you"* (Mav GPT) [13].
* **Subject Repeater + Future State Change**: e.g., *"Claude just changed social media forever"* (Kallaway) [13].

#### Strict Copywriting Rules
* **Radical Specificity**: Use exact numbers and dollars over general terms (e.g., *"\$97,000 in 13 days on Instagram"* rather than *"several thousand in a few weeks"*; *"22 days"* instead of *"a few weeks"*) [14].
* **Power Words & Phrases**: Use 1–3 word clusters that act as "heat-seeking missiles" for attention (e.g., *"heat-seeking missiles"*, *"social media machine"*) [14, 15].
* **Line Limit & Phrasing Breaks**: 
  * If using basic **system fonts**, stick to a **2-line maximum** [16]. 
  * Line breaks must split along natural phrasing pauses. For example, write line 1 as *"ChatGPT just pioneered"* and line 2 as *"the future of work"* (never break intact phrases like *"the future of work"* across lines) [16, 17].
  * **3 lines** are only acceptable with premium typography where one line is heavily emphasized in size over the others [17].
* **No Punctuation**: Omit all punctuation except quotation marks or parentheses [17].
* **No Transition Words**: Never include words like *and*, *or*, *that*, *but*, or *therefore*—write punchy trigger words, not prose [17].
* **The 3-Second Rule**: Keep the title text on screen for at least **3 seconds** so the viewer has time to look into your eyes, scan the text, absorb the visuals, and re-read [18].

---

### 5. Spoken Hooks & Power Word Remixing
Spoken hooks combine a **Hook Format** (grammatical structure) with **Power Words** [19]. 

* **Format Example**: *"Here's how to [do X bigger task] in [Y shorter time]"* (e.g., *"Here's how to plan your next 30 days of content in 30 minutes"*) [20].
* **Power Word Remixing**: Rather than copying viral lines verbatim, extract high-performing power phrases and substitute words while keeping the psychological tension intact [20, 21]:
  * *Original Phrase*: *"Scientifically impossible to skip"* [20].
  * *Remixed Variants*: *"Neurochemically impossible to skip"*, *"Psychologically impossible to resist"*, or *"Scientifically impossible to ignore"* [21].
  * *Machine Metaphor*: *"Turn Claude into a social media machine"* can be remixed into an *"email marketing machine"* or *"LinkedIn machine"* [15].

---

### 6. Visual Hook Categories & Execution
Visual hooks stun the viewer into pausing [22]. They fall into five categories [22, 23]:
1. **Graphic & Text Overlays**: Placing graphics or title text over the base footage [22].
2. **Pattern Interrupts / Visual Switching**: Switching from the speaker to another visual to create a "stun gun" effect [22].
3. **Subject Motion**: Physical movement of the subject into or out of the frame [22].
4. **Visual Effects / Transitions**: Adding stylized effects on top of footage [23].
5. **Visual Selection**: Selecting specific, highly intriguing visuals that trigger a freeze [23].

*80/20 Rule for Beginners*: Avoid overly gimmicky setups [24, 25]. Stick to moving your body in frame (a slight lean-in), moving a visual element, or sliding text on top [24, 25].

---

### 7. The "Lock-In Zone" (The Critical 5–10 Seconds)
While the hook gets the initial freeze, the **Lock-In Zone**—the **2 to 4 sentences (5–10 seconds)** directly following the hook—is where you actually earn the viewer's attention for the rest of the video [25, 26]. 

The Lock-In Zone performs two vital psychological functions [26, 27]:
1. **Confirming the Hook Claim**: Reassures the viewer that they are not being bait-and-switched [27].
2. **Rapid Trust Evaluation**: Viewers instantly evaluate whether the creator is credible or going to waste their time [27].

#### Four Elements of the Lock-In Zone
To build immediate trust during these crucial seconds, leverage four anchors [27, 28]:
* **Messenger Attractiveness / Appearance**: Presenting yourself as visually polished or attractive enhances initial retention [28].
* **Packaging Quality**: Crisp framing, lighting, set design, clear audio, and visual polish exude effort—and viewers equate care with trust [28, 29] (e.g., creators like Jesse Jean, who shoot simple talking-head videos at home that still feel high-quality) [29].
* **Relatability**: Matching viewer expectations regarding demographics, style, and tone [29]. Gen Z audiences often prefer Gen Z creators for AI content, whereas accounting advice carries more weight coming from someone fitting a traditional professional image [30].
* **Proof / The Trust Anchor (Most Important)**: Showing immediate concrete proof—such as a data screenshot, case study, or study reference—proves your claim is real right away [30].

---
